simple: One of the ten symbols 0 to 9 that we use to write numbers.
analogy: A single count of beans, cups or bowls on the table: never more than nine of one kind.
precise: A symbol standing for a whole number from 0 to 9; a base-ten numeral is a row of digits.
source: D1 of F0-11 (pending verification; arithmetic checked by the chapter's number-check run)

simple: What a digit is worth because of where it stands in the number.
analogy: A loose bean is worth one, a cup ten beans, a bowl a hundred.
precise: In base ten, the place k steps left of the ones place is worth 10 multiplied by itself k times; a digit's value is the digit times its place value. Places to the right of the decimal point are worth 1/10, 1/100, ...
source: D1 of F0-11 (pending verification; arithmetic checked by the chapter's number-check run)

simple: A number written as the sum of what each digit is worth.
analogy: Saying "3 bowls and 4 cups and 7 beans" instead of 347.
precise: The sum of each digit times its place value, for example 3,407 = 3,000 + 400 + 0 + 7.
source: D1 of F0-11 (pending verification; arithmetic checked by the chapter's number-check run)

simple: A zero that keeps the other digits in their right places.
analogy: An empty cup spot on the table that says "no cups here".
precise: A digit 0 in a numeral; it adds nothing to the value but fixes the position, and so the place value, of every digit to its left.
source: D1 of F0-11 (pending verification; arithmetic checked by the chapter's number-check run)

simple: A thousand thousands.
analogy: A thousand bowls of a thousand beans each.
precise: 1,000,000 = 1,000 × 1,000, a 1 followed by six zeros. In this university a billion means a thousand millions, 1,000,000,000.
source: D1 of F0-11 (pending verification; arithmetic checked by the chapter's number-check run)

simple: The answer when you add.
analogy: Putting two piles of rice together into one pile.
precise: The result of addition; 12 is the sum of 7 and 5.
source: D1 of F0-12 (pending verification; arithmetic checked by the chapter's number-check run)

simple: The answer when you take away; how far apart two numbers are.
analogy: How many more spoons one jar holds than another.
precise: The result of subtraction; 12 − 5 = 7.
source: D1 of F0-12 (pending verification; arithmetic checked by the chapter's number-check run)

simple: The answer when you multiply.
analogy: The rice in many spoons when each spoon holds the same number of grains.
precise: The result of multiplication; for whole numbers 3 × 4 means 4 + 4 + 4 = 12.
source: D1 of F0-12 (pending verification; arithmetic checked by the chapter's number-check run)

simple: The answer when you divide: how many in each share, or how many shares.
analogy: How many full cars of four children you can make.
precise: The result of division; in whole-number division 23 ÷ 4 has quotient 5 and remainder 3.
source: D1 of F0-12 (pending verification; arithmetic checked by the chapter's number-check run)

simple: What is left over when things do not share out exactly.
analogy: The three children still waiting after five cars are full.
precise: For whole numbers a and b (b not zero), the r with a = quotient × b + r and 0 ≤ r < b; 23 = 5 × 4 + 3. C++ computes it with %.
source: D1 of F0-12 (pending verification; arithmetic checked by the chapter's number-check run)

simple: The agreed order for doing the steps of a calculation.
analogy: A recipe that says "mix the dry things first, then add the milk".
precise: Brackets first; then multiplication and division from left to right; then addition and subtraction from left to right.
source: D1 of F0-12 (pending verification; arithmetic checked by the chapter's number-check run)

simple: Swapping a number for a nearby friendly one.
analogy: Saying "about 90 grains" when you counted 87.
precise: Replacing a number by the nearest multiple of 10 (or 100, 1,000, ...); in this university a number exactly halfway rounds up (45 → 50).
source: D1 of F0-12 (pending verification; arithmetic checked by the chapter's number-check run)

simple: A sensible "about" answer you can get quickly.
analogy: Guessing the rice in a jar from one spoonful.
precise: An approximate result, usually found by rounding the inputs before calculating; used to check exact answers.
source: D1 of F0-12 (pending verification; arithmetic checked by the chapter's number-check run)

simple: Taking the next whole number when anything is left over, so that everything fits.
analogy: One more car for the last three children.
precise: The smallest whole number of groups of size b that holds a items; with whole-number division, (a + b − 1) ÷ b. Also called ceiling division. It is the number of blocks in a GPU launch (F6).
source: D1 of F0-12; R1 of F0-12 (pending verification; arithmetic checked by the chapter's number-check run)

simple: A number that says "this many parts out of that many equal parts".
analogy: 3 slices of a bread cut into 8 equal slices.
precise: A number a/b with whole numbers a and b, b not zero; it means a ÷ b.
source: D1 of F0-13 (pending verification; arithmetic checked by the chapter's number-check run)

simple: The top number of a fraction: how many parts you have.
analogy: The slices Hana ate.
precise: a in the fraction a/b.
source: D1 of F0-13 (pending verification; arithmetic checked by the chapter's number-check run)

simple: The bottom number of a fraction: how many equal parts make the whole.
analogy: How many slices the bread was cut into.
precise: b in the fraction a/b; it must not be zero.
source: D1 of F0-13 (pending verification; arithmetic checked by the chapter's number-check run)

simple: Different-looking fractions that are the same amount.
analogy: Half a bread is the same as 4 slices out of 8.
precise: a/b and c/d are equivalent when a × d = b × c; multiplying or dividing top and bottom by the same non-zero number gives an equivalent fraction.
source: D1 of F0-13 (pending verification; arithmetic checked by the chapter's number-check run)

simple: A number with a point, where the digits after the point are tenths, hundredths, thousandths.
analogy: Cutting each slice into ten smaller pieces, and each of those into ten again.
precise: Base-ten place value continued to the right of the ones place: places worth 1/10, 1/100, 1/1,000, ... Computers usually store such numbers in base two as close copies (MA302).
source: D1 of F0-13; R1 of F0-13 (pending verification; arithmetic checked by the chapter's number-check run)

simple: "Out of a hundred".
analogy: Pretending the bread was cut into 100 tiny equal slices and counting how many you ate.
precise: p % means p/100; 37.5 % = 0.375 = 3/8. Percentages above 100 are allowed.
source: D1 of F0-13 (pending verification; arithmetic checked by the chapter's number-check run)

simple: A number less than zero, written with a minus sign in front.
analogy: A floor below the street, or a temperature below zero.
precise: For every number a > 0, its opposite −a satisfies a + (−a) = 0; numbers below 0 are negative.
source: D1 of F0-14 (pending verification; arithmetic checked by the chapter's number-check run)

simple: A straight line where every number has its own spot, smaller on the left and bigger on the right.
analogy: The lift shaft lying on its side: street floor at 0.
precise: A line with a chosen point for 0 and a fixed spacing for 1, so that each number corresponds to one point; moving right adds, moving left takes away.
source: D1 of F0-14 (pending verification; arithmetic checked by the chapter's number-check run)

simple: A whole number that may be positive, negative or zero.
analogy: A lift button: no half floors.
precise: Any of ..., −2, −1, 0, 1, 2, ...: the whole numbers together with their opposites. Not the same as the C++ type int, which holds only a limited range of integers (MA102).
source: D1 of F0-14 (pending verification; arithmetic checked by the chapter's number-check run)

simple: The number the same distance from zero on the other side.
analogy: Floor 3 and floor −3 are both three floors from the street.
precise: The opposite of a is −a, with a + (−a) = 0; subtracting a number is adding its opposite.
source: D1 of F0-14 (pending verification; arithmetic checked by the chapter's number-check run)

simple: How many steps apart two numbers are on the number line, never negative.
analogy: How many floors the lift travels.
precise: The larger number minus the smaller one; from −4 to 3 it is 3 − (−4) = 7.
source: D1 of F0-14 (pending verification; arithmetic checked by the chapter's number-check run)

simple: A number multiplied by itself a certain number of times.
analogy: Folding paper again and again: each fold multiplies the layers by 2.
precise: For a whole number n, a^n is n copies of a multiplied together; a^0 = 1.
source: D1 of F0-15 (pending verification; arithmetic checked by the chapter's number-check run)

simple: The small raised number that says how many times to multiply.
analogy: The number of folds.
precise: n in a^n (also written a^n in plain text and program output).
source: D1 of F0-15 (pending verification; arithmetic checked by the chapter's number-check run)

simple: 1, 10, 100, 1,000 and so on: a 1 followed by zeros.
analogy: The bowls and cups of F0-11, ten of each making the next.
precise: 10^n, written as 1 followed by n zeros; the place values of base ten.
source: D1 of F0-15 (pending verification; arithmetic checked by the chapter's number-check run)

simple: 1, 2, 4, 8, 16 and so on: each one double the one before.
analogy: The layers of paper after each fold; a row of switches, each worth double the one to its right.
precise: 2^n for a whole number n; the place values of base two; n on/off switches make 2^n patterns.
source: D1 of F0-15 (pending verification; arithmetic checked by the chapter's number-check run)

simple: How many times you must double 1 to reach a number, or halve the number to get back to 1.
analogy: How many folds made 1,024 layers.
precise: log2(x) is the exponent n with 2^n = x; log2(1,024) = 10.
source: D1 of F0-15 (pending verification; arithmetic checked by the chapter's number-check run)

simple: A letter or name that stands for a number.
analogy: A labelled jar: the label is the name, the counters inside are the number.
precise: A symbol such as n that represents a number, either one not yet known or any number from a range. Not the same as a variable in a program (KID102 F0-30), which is a named storage place whose contents can change.
source: D1 of F0-16 (pending verification; arithmetic checked by the chapter's number-check run)

simple: A recipe for a number made of numbers, letters and operations, with no equals sign.
analogy: The note "2 × batches" before you know the batches.
precise: A combination of numbers, variables and operations, such as 3n + 2, that has a value once every variable has a value.
source: D1 of F0-16 (pending verification; arithmetic checked by the chapter's number-check run)

simple: Put a number in place of a letter.
analogy: Dropping counters into the labelled jar.
precise: Replace each occurrence of a variable by a given value (in brackets if needed) and evaluate with the order of operations.
source: D1 of F0-16 (pending verification; arithmetic checked by the chapter's number-check run)

simple: One piece of an expression that is added or taken away.
analogy: One line of a recipe.
precise: A product of a number (its coefficient) and variables, such as 3n; in 3n + 2 the terms are 3n and 2.
source: D1 of F0-16 (pending verification; arithmetic checked by the chapter's number-check run)

simple: Terms with exactly the same letters, which can be added together.
analogy: 4 cups of rice and 3 cups of rice make 7 cups of rice; rice and milk do not combine.
precise: Terms whose variable parts are identical; 4a + 3a = 7a, but 3a + 2b cannot be combined.
source: D1 of F0-16 (pending verification; arithmetic checked by the chapter's number-check run)

simple: A rule that says how to work out one quantity from others.
analogy: The fridge note "eggs = 2 × batches".
precise: An equation giving one variable in terms of others, such as ticket = table × seatsPerTable + seat (the F6 index formula in disguise).
source: D1 of F0-16 (pending verification; arithmetic checked by the chapter's number-check run)

simple: A statement that two amounts are equal, with an = sign in the middle.
analogy: A balance scale with its beam level.
precise: A statement expression = expression, such as 3x + 2 = 14; true for some values of its variables and false for others.
source: D1 of F0-17 (pending verification; arithmetic checked by the chapter's number-check run)

simple: The number you are trying to find.
analogy: The marbles hidden inside one closed bag.
precise: A variable in an equation whose value is to be determined, often called x.
source: D1 of F0-17 (pending verification; arithmetic checked by the chapter's number-check run)

simple: The number that makes an equation true.
analogy: The count that, put in every bag, keeps the beam level.
precise: A value of the unknown for which both sides of the equation have the same value; x = 4 solves 3x + 2 = 14.
source: D1 of F0-17 (pending verification; arithmetic checked by the chapter's number-check run)

simple: The operation that undoes another one.
analogy: Taking marbles off undoes putting them on.
precise: Subtraction undoes addition; division by a non-zero number undoes multiplication; applying the same inverse operation to both sides keeps an equation true.
source: D1 of F0-17 (pending verification; arithmetic checked by the chapter's number-check run)

simple: A rule that takes a number in and gives exactly one number out.
analogy: A kitchen gadget that always does the same thing.
precise: A rule f that assigns to every allowed input x exactly one output f(x). Not the same as a function in a program (KID102 F0-34), which is a named piece of code.
source: D1 of F0-18 (pending verification; arithmetic checked by the chapter's number-check run)

simple: What goes into a rule, and what comes out.
analogy: The time you ask about, and the distance the simulator tells you.
precise: For y = f(x), x is the input (independent variable) and y the output (dependent variable).
source: D1 of F0-18 (pending verification; arithmetic checked by the chapter's number-check run)

simple: A pair of numbers that says where a point is: across first, then up.
analogy: "Third tile from the door, fifth tile from the wall."
precise: An ordered pair (x, y): x along the horizontal axis, y along the vertical axis.
source: D1 of F0-18 (pending verification; arithmetic checked by the chapter's number-check run)

simple: One of the two number lines at the edge of a graph.
analogy: The edge of the kitchen floor where you count tiles.
precise: A number line measuring one coordinate; the horizontal and vertical axes cross at (0, 0).
source: D1 of F0-18 (pending verification; arithmetic checked by the chapter's number-check run)

simple: A picture of a function made of all its points.
analogy: Dots on squared paper, one per row of a table.
precise: The set of points (x, f(x)) for all allowed inputs x, drawn on a pair of axes.
source: D1 of F0-18 (pending verification; arithmetic checked by the chapter's number-check run)

simple: How much the output changes when the input goes up by 1.
analogy: How many centimetres the robot moves each second.
precise: For y = mx + c, the number m; between two points, (change in y) ÷ (change in x). It can be negative.
source: D1 of F0-18 (pending verification; arithmetic checked by the chapter's number-check run)

simple: A statement that one amount is bigger or smaller than another.
analogy: A balance scale that is tipped, not level.
precise: A statement using <, >, ≤, ≥ or ≠, such as x + 3 ≤ 7; multiplying or dividing both sides by a negative number reverses it.
source: D1 of F0-19 (pending verification; arithmetic checked by the chapter's number-check run)

simple: All the numbers that are permitted, from a lowest to a highest.
analogy: The jar spots that exist on the shelf: 0 to 9.
precise: The set of values satisfying one or more inequalities; the half-open range 0 ≤ i < n holds exactly n whole numbers, 0 to n − 1.
source: D1 of F0-19 (pending verification; arithmetic checked by the chapter's number-check run)

simple: Checking that a number is inside the allowed range before using it.
analogy: "Is my ticket less than 10?" before walking to the shelf.
precise: A test such as if (i < n) that guards every use of position i in a list of n items numbered from 0; every GPU kernel whose grid can exceed its data needs one (guide 13.4).
source: D1 and R1 of F0-19 (pending verification; arithmetic checked by the chapter's number-check run)

simple: A mistake that makes a count or a range one too big or one too small.
analogy: Letting ticket 10 walk to a shelf that ends at 9.
precise: An error at the edge of a range, for example using ≤ where < is needed, or counting the ends of a range wrongly.
source: D1 and R3 of F0-19 (pending verification; arithmetic checked by the chapter's number-check run)
